query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy with varying grain sizes using different processing routes, such as high-pressure torsion or annealing. Measure the compressive strength, ductility, and caloric response of each sample.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the grain size refinement does not lead to improved integrity, as measured by compressive strength and ductility, without sacrificing caloric response, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: While the yield strength and KJIc fracture toughness of the medium-entropy CrCoNi and high-entropy CrMnFeCoNi alloys are comparable, the tensile strengths, tensile ductility and work of fracture of the CrCoNi alloy are significantly higher, by respectively ∼15, ∼30 and ∼50%, at room temperature. At cryogenic temperatures, the strengths of the two alloys are comparable (σUTS∼1,300 MPa at 77 K), but the KJIc fracture toughness, tensile ductility and work of fracture are again markedly higher in the CrCoNi alloy, by ∼25, ∼27 and ∼31%, respectively. The yield strength, σy, at 77 K is slightly below that of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy, which we believe is due to the non-uniform grain size of our present material (Fig. 1b–d). Consistent with this notion, in a previous study where the grain size of CrCoNi was uniform and comparable to that of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy, the tensile properties of the three-component alloy were found to exceed those of the five-component alloy at all temperatures.

Such damage-tolerant properties of the CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy are literally unprecedented for mechanical behaviour at cryogenic temperatures. For a material with a tensile strength of 1.3 GPa to display ductilities (failure strains) of 90%, and ‘valid' crack-growth fracture toughnesses that exceeds 430 MPa m1/2, all at liquid-nitrogen temperatures, is exceptional and clearly exceed the excellent cryogenic properties of our previously reported CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy. Its ductility compares favourably to high-Mn twinning-induced plasticity steels and strength and toughness are comparable to the very best cryogenic steels, for example, certain austenitic stainless steels and high-Ni steels; in addition, the strength, ductility and toughness of the CrCoNi alloy exceed the properties of all medium- and high-entropy alloys reported to date (Fig. 4). Moreover, with a uniformly fine grain size, it is eminently feasible that the strength, ductility and toughness properties of this CrCoNi alloy may further improve. AbstractAnnealing of severely plastic deformed materials is expected to produce a good combination of strength and ductility, which has been widely demonstrated in conventional materials. In the present study, high-pressure torsion processed CoCrNi medium entropy alloy consisting of a single face-centered cubic (FCC) phase with a grain size of ~50 nm was subjected to different annealing conditions, and its effect on microstructure and mechanical behavior was investigated. The annealing of high-pressure torsion processed CoCrNi alloy exhibits partial recrystallization and near full recrystallization based on the annealing temperature and time. The samples annealed at 700 °C for 2 min exhibit very fine grain size, a high fraction of low angle grain boundaries, and high kernel average misorientation value, indicating partially recrystallized microstructure. The samples annealed for a longer duration (>2 min) exhibit relatively larger grain size, a low fraction of low angle grain boundaries, and low kernel average misorientation value, indicating nearly full recrystallized microstructure. decision.trend: The trend in the research on high-entropy alloys is towards improving their mechanical properties, such as strength and ductility, while maintaining their unique characteristics, such as high caloric response. Researchers have been exploring various approaches, including changing the composition, processing routes, and microstructure architecture. The use of epoxy-containing composites and low-melting In composites has shown promise in improving compressive strength and thermal conductivity, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved.
decision.unsolved: The unsolved problem is to achieve a high-entropy alloy with both robust integrity and high caloric performance without sacrificing one for the other. The current approaches have shown improvements in either strength or heat transport metrics, but not simultaneously.
decision.why: Grain size refinement has been shown to improve the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys, such as strength and ductility. By refining the grain size, it may be possible to achieve a better balance between robust integrity and high caloric performance. This approach is supported by prior evidence, such as the work on refractory high-entropy alloys, which showed improved yield strengths and ductility with reduced grain size.
